1.q: בִּ⁠שְׁנַ֨ת בֹּ֤א תַרְתָּן֙ אַשְׁדּ֔וֹדָ⁠ה בִּ⁠שְׁלֹ֣ח אֹת֔⁠וֹ סַֽרְג֖וֹן מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֑וּר וַ⁠יִּלָּ֥חֶם בְּ⁠אַשְׁדּ֖וֹד וַֽ⁠יִּלְכְּדָֽ⁠הּ
1.note: Isaiah is using **In the year of the coming of the Tartan to Ashdod, when Sargon, the king of Assyria, sent him, and he fought against Ashdod and captured it** to describe something that was ongoing at this time. This provides the background for other events he will describe that began to happen during this time. Connect this clause to the story in a way that makes it clear in your language that this clause is describing something that was ongoing in the background. Alternate translation: [During the time when the Tartan came to Ashdod, after Sargon, the king of Assyria, sent him, and he fought against Ashdod and captured it]

A **Tartan** is an Assyrian military title for the supreme commander of the army. If your readers would not be familiar with what a Tartan is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the supreme commander]

2.note: Here, **by the hand of Isaiah** represents “through Isaiah.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [through Isaiah]

**Going naked and barefoot** was a symbolic action by which Isaiah showed that Yahweh would bring judgment on Egypt and Cush. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [going naked and barefoot to show that Yahweh would bring judgment on Egypt and Cush]

Here, **hand** represents the capability of Isaiah to serve Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh conveyed a message through Isaiah]

3.q: כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר הָלַ֛ךְ עַבְדִּ֥⁠י יְשַׁעְיָ֖הוּ עָר֣וֹם וְ⁠יָחֵ֑ף
3.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **my servant Isaiah has gone naked and barefoot**, so will the people of Egypt and Cush be led away naked and barefoot as captives. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [My servant Isaiah has gone naked and barefoot to show that the people of Egypt and Cush will be led away naked and barefoot]

Going **naked and barefoot three years** was a symbolic action by which Isaiah showed that the people of Egypt and Cush would be taken away as captives. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [like a captive for three years]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **a sign** and **a wonder**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [to show and to warn what would come against]

The terms **sign** and **wonder** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [a remarkable sign against]

4.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **captivity** and **exile**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [those taken captive from Egypt and those exiled from Cush]

The terms **captivity** and **exile** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the exiled captives of Egypt and Cush]

Here, **the exile of Cush** represents “the exiled people of Cush.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the exiled people of Cush]

Yahweh is referring to all of the people by naming two major components, **young men** and **old ones**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all the people, both young and old]

Yahweh is referring to the full nakedness of the captives in a polite way by using the phrase **uncovered of buttock**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [and with their buttocks exposed]

Here, **the nakedness of Egypt** represents “the humiliation of Egypt.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the humiliation of Egypt]

5.note: The terms **dismay** and **shame** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [And they will be utterly ashamed]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **dismay** and **shame**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [And they will be dismayed and ashamed]

Yahweh is speaking of Cush as if it were **their hope**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of Cush, the nation in which they had hoped]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **hope** and **glory**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [because of Cush, the nation in which they had hoped, and because of Egypt, the nation of which they were proud]

Yahweh is speaking of Egypt as if it were **their glory**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Egypt, the nation in which they had taken pride]

6.q: וְ֠⁠אָמַר יֹשֵׁ֨ב הָ⁠אִ֣י הַ⁠זֶּה֮ בַּ⁠יּ֣וֹם הַ⁠הוּא֒ הִנֵּה־כֹ֣ה מַבָּטֵ֗⁠נוּ אֲשֶׁר־נַ֤סְנוּ שָׁם֙ לְ⁠עֶזְרָ֔ה לְ⁠הִ֨נָּצֵ֔ל מִ⁠פְּנֵ֖י מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֑וּר וְ⁠אֵ֖יךְ נִמָּלֵ֥ט אֲנָֽחְנוּ
6.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And the dweller of this coastland will say in that day that that was their hope, where they fled for help, to be delivered from the face of the king of Assyria, and that there was no way for them to escape.]

The dweller of this coastland is speaking as if his listeners could see what he is about to describe by saying **Behold**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Indeed]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **hope**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [was the one we were counting on]

The expression **to be delivered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [so that they would deliver us]

Here, **the face of the king of Assyria** represents “the presence of the king of Assyria.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the presence of the king of Assyria]

The dweller of this coastland is using the question form to emphasize that there is no way to escape. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And there is no way for us to escape!]

The people of the coastland are stating the pronoun **we** separately, even though the verb translated as **will we escape** already includes this meaning. They are doing that to emphasize their personal alarm, since the nations they hoped would protect them are now being defeated by the king of Assyria. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [So then what about us? How will we ever escape]
